newsitem.title: GERMANY: BUBA OFFICIAL SEES GERMAN RATES STEADY NEAR TERM.
newsitem.headline: BUBA OFFICIAL SEES GERMAN RATES STEADY NEAR TERM.

text.p: German interest rates are likely to remain steady for some time, but this does not rule out the chance of another possible easing at a later date, a senior Bundesbank official said on Wednesday.

Explaining that inflationary pressures in Germany were currently modest and showed no signs of increasing soon, Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick said, "There is currently no pressure to raise interest rates."

In fact "many factors would support a policy of keeping interest rates steady for the time being," Koebnick, also president of the state central bank in the Rhineland and Saar regions, told Reuters in an interview.
Koebnick also said that there was currently no reason to lower the central bank's main money market rate, the repo, set at three percent.

After the Bundesbank unexpectedly slashed 30 basis points off the repo rate in late August, some market participants had set their hopes on another possible easing, particularly since inflation rates continue to be very moderate.
The Bundesbank's other two key rates, the discount and Lombard rates, were cut by 50 basis points to 2.50 percent and 4.50 percent respectively in April.
Looking ahead, Koebnick said the fact that German interest rates were currently at historic lows should not be seen to prohibit another rate cut in the future.
"This does not rule out the fact that a situation could arise in which the Bundesbank, while keeping its price goal in mind, could lower rates again," Koebnick said.
Conditions for another easing may improve, if M3 money supply, the central bank's key policy indicator, continues to grow more slowly, several Bundesbank officials have said in recent weeks.

In August M3, measuring 8.7 percent on an annualised, seasonally adjusted basis, grew more rapidly than it did in July, but Koebnick remained optimistic that growth will continue to slow and maybe even hit the target corridor soon.
"The tendency is still for M3 to approach the (four to seven percent) corridor," Koebnick said, adding that growth should "certainly be below eight percent" soon.
